suggested_english: I am struggling to breathe and my lips have changed colour
suggestion_note: PARITY CORRECTION, and it now runs the other way. When I first checked, the speaker's EX04 third said 'ubururu' (blue) while the first said 'ibara' (colour); the Kinyarwanda has since been made consistent and BOTH persons now say 'ibara'. So English/French/Swahili naming blue is a three-against-one against a Kinyarwanda that is now internally settled, and under the ruling the English follows the patient's report. Dropping 'blue' also separates EX04 cleanly from CR03, whose speaker text IS 'Iminwa yanjye yahindutse ubururu' — the two concepts were only distinguishable by that word.

suggested_english: My child's ear is hurting and there is fluid coming out
suggestion_note: HOLD LIFTED — the Kinyarwanda hold is a pure vocabulary blocker and does not transfer. Section 7 records it: no ear term is attested anywhere in the approved Kinyarwanda ('ugutwi' appears in none of the speaker's phrases, none of vocabulary.py, none of the review sheet), so the row cannot be written in Kinyarwanda without the speaker supplying a word. English has no such gap. This is exactly the case the brief's carry-over rule anticipated: inherit the hold, then lift it where the reason is Kinyarwanda wording rather than the concept. RULE 12 NOTE: first person here is the CARER, not the child — the parent reports the child's ear.

suggestion_note: gloss 'child growth monitoring visit'. Matches the speaker's own 'Ndashaka ko bapima ibiro by'umwana wanjye.' Rule 12: the requester is the carer, so first person is the parent, not the child.

ADULT_RELATIONS, not CHILD_RELATIONS — group A: the carer speaks and the child stays lexical. So {REL} is the adult and 'their child' is the patient, matching the speaker's '{REL} ashaka ko bapima ibiro by'umwana we.' Singular 'their' per the ruling, and it does double duty here: it is both gender-neutral and the possessive the Kinyarwanda 'we' carries.
